title: The garden
hookLine: what no eye has seen or ear heard

lines: RED, TO SOMEONE WHO NEVER SAW COLOR.
cards: Try describing the color red to someone who has never seen color. You can say warm, you can say fire, you can say the inside of a pomegranate. Every word points, and none of them arrives.
The Qur'an describes the garden of paradise with rivers, shade, fruit and peace. And then the tradition does something unexpected. It says, in effect: whatever you're picturing, it's more than that.

teach.b: The Arabic word is jannah, a garden, and the Qur'an pictures it in many passages: gardens with rivers flowing beneath, shade that doesn't fade, fruit within reach, greetings of peace.
Then comes a hadith qudsi, a saying the Prophet, peace be upon him, reports from Allah.

teach.h: NO EYE, NO EAR, NO HEART.
teach.b: In Sahih al-Bukhari, Allah says: I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has never occurred to a human heart. Three doors, all closed.
Not the eye, not the ear, not even imagination. In the same report, the companion Abu Hurayrah adds: recite, if you like, this verse.

teach.h: KEPT HID: A JOY BEYOND THE PICTURE.
teach.b: In Pickthall's translation: "No soul knoweth what is kept hid for them of joy, as a reward for what they used to do." Kept hid.
So the Qur'an's descriptions are real, and Muslims take them seriously, but they're also signposts, pointing at a joy bigger than the pointing.

Scholars have discussed how literally to read the garden's details, and they've answered in more than one way. But this hadith keeps everyone humble: whatever your picture is, it's smaller than the thing.
So the garden isn't a catalog to be calculated.
It's a hope that stays open, and the best joy you've tasted is a hint, not the whole.

how: Muslims affirm the garden (jannah) as part of belief in the Last Day; teachers often pair the Qur'an's descriptions with the hadith qudsi that it holds what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no heart has imagined.

o: paradise: a joy beyond anything eye, ear or heart has known
a quiet orchard a family keeps as charity for travelers
the walled courtyard garden planted around a great mosque

p: no eye, no ear, no heart
what Allah prepared is beyond all three
added: recite the verse if you like

s: the hadith says paradise is exactly what people picture
it says it holds what no eye has seen and what has never occurred to a human heart.
Abu Hurayrah linked the hadith to a verse of the Qur'an
he pointed to the verse: no soul knoweth what is kept hid for them of joy.
scholars have read the garden's details in more than one way
they have discussed how literally to read them, without one single answer.

games.q: you're asked to describe paradise in full, using the hadith. what can you honestly say?
o: it's beyond what any eye, ear or heart has known.
nothing at all can be said.
games.why: the Qur'an gives real pictures, and the hadith says what is prepared goes beyond them all.

practice: Bring to mind one moment of real joy, a laugh at a kitchen table, cool water on a hot day, someone's face lighting up when they saw you, and let the light and sounds fill in for a few breaths.

Then hold the hadith beside it, no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and let your joy be a hint pointing past itself. If you pray, thank Allah for that moment with alhamdulillah; if not, let it be a plain thank-you.

wordCard.voice: The garden. Jannah: paradise in the Qur'an, rivers and shade and peace, and in the hadith, a joy that no eye has seen and no heart has imagined. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a garden; the Qur'an's word for paradise.

carryVoice: Your line: no eye has seen. Whatever you picture, it's more. Go gently.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3244 (hadith qudsi: what no eye has seen, no ear has heard)
